title: VII. Third plague: outward operations cease; Tatian, Tertullian, Nyssen, Bernard, Durandus
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the soul cannot stand as moved from place to place by reason of operation. But the separated soul stands as not said to have any operation around a place, or around a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it stands as determined toward a certain body, it cannot move nor act upon another except by means belonging toward its own body, but it lacks that while it stands as separated. Angels stand as said to stand as moved from place to place insofar as they operate successively in diverse places. So Durandus, whom Pico della Mirandola follows. And again, where the body shall stand as wanting, there will stand as no delusion. The spirit belonging toward a human being without the body can neither itself advance nor profit another, as Bernard authorizes in Song of Songs sermon 5. The soul alone does nothing, says Nyssen in the first oration On the Resurrection. Deeds stand as administered through the flesh. but for accomplishing, it awaits the service belonging toward the flesh. For from its own it has only to think, to will, to desire; The soul from its own resources scarcely suffices for acting, says Tertullian in On the Resurrection chapter 46. how would souls stand as operative after death? Tatian by that argument proves that souls do not become demons: For that the state belonging toward the soul severed from the body stands as imperfect, and that it has no act, has seemed so to many holy men. The third plague belonging toward the soul in death stands as that by which it extinguishes all its operations, especially those outward. VII.
pass_b_english: VII. The third plague of the soul in death is that by which it extinguishes all its operations, especially those outward. For that the state of the soul severed from the body is imperfect, and that it has no act, has seemed so to many holy men. Tatian by that argument proves that souls do not become demons: how would souls be operative after death? The soul from its own resources scarcely suffices for acting, says Tertullian in On the Resurrection chapter 46. For from its own it has only to think, to will, to desire; but for accomplishing, it awaits the service of the flesh. Deeds are administered through the flesh. The soul alone does nothing, says Nyssen in the first oration On the Resurrection. The spirit of a human being without the body can neither itself advance nor profit another, as Bernard authorizes in Song of Songs sermon 5. And again, where the body shall be wanting, there will be no delusion. So Durandus, whom Pico della Mirandola follows. Angels are said to be moved from place to place insofar as they operate successively in diverse places. But the separated soul is not said to have any operation around a place, or around a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it is determined to a certain body, it cannot move nor act upon another except by means of its own body, but it lacks that while it is separated. Therefore the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of operation.
source_text: VII. Tertia animae in morte plaga est, qua omnes operationes ejus, quae sunt praesertim ad extra, exstinguit. Nam imperfectum esse animae statum a corpore sejunctae, & nullum habere actum, multis sanctis viris visum est. Tatianus enim eo argumento probat animas non fieri daemones: quomodo forent animae operatrices post mortem? Anima ad agendum de suo minime sufficit, inquit Tertullianus lib. de resurr. cap. 46. Habet enim de suo solummodo cogitare, velle, cupere; ad perficiendum autem, operam carnis exspectat. Facta per carnem administrantur. Anima sola nihil facit, inquit Nyssenus orat. 1. de resurr. Spiritus hominis absque corpore nec ipse proficere, nec alteri prodesse potest, auctore Bernardo in Cant. serm. 5. Iterumque, ubi deerit corpus, delus non erit. Ita Durandus, quem Johannes Picus de Mirandula sequitur. Angeli dicuntur moveri de loco in locum, in quantum successive operantur in diversis locis. Anima autem separata non dicitur habere aliquam operationem circa locum, vel circa corpus existens in loco, quia cum ex natura sua sit determinata ad certum corpus, non potest movere, nec agere in aliud nisi mediante corpore proprio, sed illo caret, dum est separata. Ergo non potest anima moveri de loco ad locum ratione operationis.
